_README: Cinema Studio 4.0, rebuilt end to end in ComfyUI: BUILD -> ATTACH -> DIRECT -> SHOOT ->
JUDGE -> POST, in one graph, with the Cinematographer's verdict exposed at the end of the
judge stage for the app to act on.
ComfyUI API-format workflow. Node category: Cinematographer.
STATUS: STRUCTURALLY VALIDATED, NOT EXECUTED. This graph has never been run. No ComfyUI
instance, no GPU and none of the weights below were available where it was written, so
nothing here is a claim that it works, that it produces a clip, or that the judgement
agrees with a human. What IS verified you can re-run yourself:
python3 workflows/validate_graphs.py
That checks the file parses as JSON, that every node has class_type + inputs, that every
class_type is in a table of slot counts, that every link resolves to an existing node id
and a slot that node declares, that every node supplies a legal number of inputs for its
class_type, that the graph is acyclic, and that every node is reachable from an output
node. It does NOT check that ComfyUI accepts the prompt. Treat the first run as a
debugging session.
ALL TEN NON-CORE NODES ARE NOW READ FROM SOURCE; NONE ARE DECLARED. The six Element and
POST nodes landed in app/cinematographer/nodes.py while this file was being written, and
the four Director's Panel nodes (CinemaDirectorPanel, CinemaCameraMove, CinemaEmotionWheel,
CinemaPromptCompose) landed afterwards. Every input name, slot count and default below is
read from that file, not guessed, and the validator's NOTE about declared slot counts is now
GONE because the set it named is empty. That is not a cosmetic change: when the four nodes
landed, all four were wired wrongly, and the name check caught them.
THE ENGINE IS A PURE DESCRIPTION LAYER, AND THAT SHAPES THIS WHOLE GRAPH. Every one of the
ten landed nodes is stdlib-only and never touches a pixel. That is a deliberate design
choice, not an omission, and it has three consequences a reader must know before reading
the wiring:
- CinemaElementSave takes an image PATH (STRING), not an IMAGE tensor. So the BUILD
stills are written to disk by SaveImage, and the path is a widget the app fills in.
- CinemaGrade, CinemaExtend and CinemaEdit take NO image input and return NO image.
They emit PLANS -- grade_json, extend_json, edit_json -- and the module comment in
nodes.py says their summaries say 'plan', never 'graded'. CinemaGradeApply is the
EXCEPTION and the only node in the pack that changes pixels: it takes the rendered
IMAGE plus CinemaGrade.grade_json and returns a graded IMAGE, which this graph writes
with SaveImage. So the GRADE is applied; the EXTEND and the EDIT are still only
described. That asymmetry is real and is not smoothed over here.
exposes the descriptions on output nodes. Applying them is the app's job, and this
README would be lying if it said otherwise.
- CinemaElementLoad returns an asset PATH (STRING), and a STRING cannot be linked into
LoadImage.image. The reason is narrower than it looks, and the obvious summary of it is
wrong, so here it is exactly. LoadImage.image declares its type as a raw LIST of
filenames (nodes.py:1754), and validate_node_input rejects when the INPUT's declared
type is not a string -- `if not isinstance(received_type, str) or not
isinstance(input_type, str): return False`. It is the INPUT being a list that rejects,
not the output. The function even tolerates the opposite direction explicitly: a
list-valued OUTPUT into a COMBO input returns True. Verified by executing the real
function, not by reading it.
That distinction matters, because it means the link is not impossible -- only
impossible from a STRING. An output typed `*` (AnyType) DOES pass, since the AnyType
check runs before the list guard. So 'resolve an Element and load it' IS expressible:
it would need CinemaElementLoad to expose a second output typed ("*",). That is a
design call for the node's owner, not something a graph can reach from outside, and an
`*` output bypasses type checking entirely, so it is a real trade rather than a free
win. This graph does not use it. Instead the first frame comes from the BUILD stage's
own in-memory IMAGE, and CinemaElementLoad is a PRE-FLIGHT CHECK -- it resolves the
name and reports `found` -- rather than the thing that feeds the sampler. The Element
registry reaches the pixels through the PROMPT (the @Name tags composed by
CinemaPromptCompose), which is exactly the product's own mechanism.
THE GATE IS A REAL DATA DEPENDENCY, AND THIS FILE PREVIOUSLY SAID IT WAS NOT.
Correction first, because the earlier claim was wrong and was repeated three times: an
earlier draft of this README asserted that CinemaGrade had no `corrections` input and that
the gate was therefore positional. THAT WAS A STALE READ. `nodes` added an optional
`corrections` STRING to CinemaGrade, and this file kept repeating a read taken before it
landed -- without re-reading the source. Executing cls.INPUT_TYPES() settles it:
CinemaGrade  required temperature, contrast, saturation, sharpness, film_grain,
highlights, exposure   (7 FLOAT)
optional corrections STRING
-> grade_json, is_neutral, summary
CinemaGradeApply  required image IMAGE, grade_json STRING, seed INT
-> image, summary   (the only node in the pack that changes pixels)
So the gate is wired as a LINK, not as a neighbourhood:
CinematographerCorrection.corrections -> CinemaGrade.corrections   (the verdict)
CinemaGrade.grade_json                -> CinemaGradeApply.grade_json
VAEDecodeTiled.image                  -> CinemaGradeApply.image     (the rendered frames)
CinemaGradeApply.image                -> SaveImage                 (the graded frame)
The judge's verdict therefore reaches POST as data. If the verdict is empty the grade is
neutral; if it carries corrections they are the grade's input. The chain terminates in a
written file, so the gate is not merely described -- it is on the pixel path.
Be clear about what a gate is here, though. ComfyUI has no conditional execution in API
format without a switch node, so a FAIL verdict does not STOP the render; it travels into
POST as text and shapes the grade. A data dependency is not a branch, and this README will
not call it one.
This is also why the validator now asserts the edge itself. A name check proves a link is
LEGAL; it cannot prove the link is PRESENT, because `corrections` is optional and deleting
the edge violates nothing. Deleting the gate produced a clean PASS until the edge assertion
was added -- found by deliberately breaking the graph and watching it still pass.
WHAT THE FIVE STAGES ARE, AND WHAT EACH ONE ACTUALLY DOES HERE:
BUILD   Generates two stills with Flux.1 [schnell] (Apache-2.0): a character reference
and a location clean plate, and writes both to disk with SaveImage. This is the
local stand-in for the product's image mode. On the model choice the TIER
matters, and an earlier draft of this README got it wrong: the T1 catalogue
lists SIX image models on the platform -- GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, Nano Banana
Pro, Flux 2, Seedream 5, GPT Image 2 and Ideogram 4.5 -- and GPT Image 2.5
Sunburst is the TUTORIALS' preference (T3), not a product mandate. We pick
Flux.1 [schnell] because it is Apache-2.0 and runs locally, and it is a sibling
of Flux 2, which the platform itself offers. So this is a licence-driven choice
inside the product's own model surface, not the substitution of something
foreign. Flux schnell is 4 steps at CFG 1.0.
ATTACH  Registers each still as a named, categorised Element (character / location /
prop). This is the product's load-bearing idea: an asset is created once and
tagged thereafter. Two CinemaElementSave calls, each writing a sidecar and
updating the project registry.
DIRECT  Sets the Director's Panel: film setup (genre, era, tempo), camera (body, lens,
aperture), the camera-move stack, and the Emotion Wheel. Every value is a widget
on a node, so every value is explicit and reproducible -- which is the point.
The product's own pitch is that a text-only prompt 'returns a different move on
every run because speed, path, and end position stay unspecified'; fixing those
properties as settings is the mechanism.
SHOOT   Composes the prompt from the action text plus the panel, the move stack, the
emotion direction and the Element registry, then generates with LTX 2.5 and
muxes to mp4. The loader block, sampler chain and sigma schedules are copied
verbatim from reshoot_ltx25.json, itself flattened from the official Lightricks
two-stage graph -- see that file's README for the provenance.
JUDGE   The Cinematographer. Seven pre-existing, already-validated nodes measuring the
directed camera pose against the framing rules and returning a pass/fail plus a
correction in metres. Its verdict is exposed on output nodes.
POST    Three plan nodes: grade, extend, edit. They DESCRIBE; they do not apply.
THE HONEST LIMIT OF THE JUDGE STAGE. The Cinematographer is arithmetic on a camera pose:
it projects a subject through an eye/target/focal-length triple and scores the geometry.
It does NOT look at the rendered pixels. It cannot, and the pack says so about itself --
measuring facial identity or reading a frame needs a vision model and is explicitly out of
scope. So JUDGE here judges the camera that was DIRECTED, not the clip that came back. It
sits between SHOOT and POST because that is where a human would look, but a reader should
not conclude that the graph inspects its own output. It does not.
The differentiator is narrower than 'it judges the result' and it survives scrutiny: we
return a MEASURED pass/fail with a correction in metres on the directed camera, where the
ecosystem's other camera tools return only presets. That is the claim, and it is true.
THE FOUR DIRECTOR NODES HAVE LANDED, AND THIS GRAPH WAS RE-CUT AGAINST THEM. The earlier
wiring used DECLARED placeholder names, because the nodes did not exist when it was cut.
When they landed, all four were wired wrongly. The validator's input-NAME check -- added the
same turn -- caught all four, which is the whole argument for checking names and not just
counts. The interface below is now read from the source that defines it (nodes.py:1688-2072),
and the COMBO values were EXECUTED against the engine (director.GENRES, prompt.CAMERA_MOVES,
...) rather than read out of a grep, because a grep across tuple boundaries silently lies:
CinemaDirectorPanel  <- genre, era, pacing, camera_model, camera_lens, camera_aperture,
light, color_palette (8 required); custom_palette,
emotion_character, emotion, emotion_intensity (4 optional)
-> panel_json, prompt_fragment, summary
CinemaCameraMove     <- prompt (required); move (optional)
-> clean_prompt, moves, unknown, ok
CinemaEmotionWheel   <- character, emotion, intensity
-> direction_json, fragment, summary
CinemaPromptCompose  <- action (required); panel_json, registry_path, moves (optional)
-> final_prompt, attachments_json, unresolved_json, ok
Two notes on the re-cut, because both are places where the obvious wiring is wrong:
* CinemaCameraMove.moves is JSON; CinemaPromptCompose.moves wants comma/newline-separated
names. Linking them is type-legal (STRING to STRING) and semantically wrong, so they are
NOT linked. CinemaPromptCompose resolves @Element/#move itself from `action`;
CinemaCameraMove is a PARALLEL resolver that reports what it found. Both read the same
text, and every output of both is exposed on a PreviewAny, so a disagreement would be
visible rather than inferred.
* CinemaDirectorPanel.panel_json is the one real data dependency in DIRECT: it feeds
CinemaPromptCompose.panel_json. The other three nodes are diagnostics.
CinemaPromptCompose imports elements.parse_element_tags rather than writing a second @/#
parser -- two parsers would drift. It emits `final_prompt` as its primary output.
One trap for whoever reads that parser, recorded here because this README is what points at
it: parse_element_tags is GREEDY to the next @/#/punctuation, so
'@Tamsin walks into @Mirror Dunes' resolves the name 'Tamsin walks into'. That is the
documented syntax and not a bug -- the delimiter has to be in the prompt.
THE CONSEQUENCE IS WORSE THAN A MIS-NAMED TAG, AND IT WAS EXECUTED, NOT REASONED ABOUT.
All four combinations, run rather than reasoned about:
case                      final_prompt                    unresolved
greedy,    NO registry    '@Tamsin walks into @helmet'     ['Tamsin walks into','helmet']
greedy,    WITH registry  '@helmet'                        ['Tamsin walks into']
delimited, NO registry    'walks into @Tamsin @helmet'     ['Tamsin','helmet']
delimited, WITH registry  'walks into @Tamsin @helmet'     []
BOTH failing paths fail, and they differ in HOW -- which is the part that changes the advice:
* WITH a registry the span is REMOVED. 'walks into' and the @Tamsin tag are gone from the
prompt entirely; they survive only in `unresolved`. Reported in the JSON, silent in the
prompt -- and the prompt is what gets rendered. This is the worse failure.
* With NO registry the span is RE-EMITTED VERBATIM as a malformed tag: final_prompt is
literally '@Tamsin walks into @helmet'. The text is still visible, but it is now a tag
the engine will never resolve. So the no-registry path is NOT the safe one.
The fix in both cases is one comma: '@Tamsin, walks into @helmet'.
THE MECHANISM, because 'the greedy parse eats prose' is the wrong explanation and the right
one is actionable. It is NOT in clean_prompt: both branches return clean_prompt == '' for the
greedy input. It is in WHICH NAMES GET RE-EMITTED AS TAGS (prompt.py:422-441):
* registry branch (line 425):  element_tags = list(resolution.names)  -- RESOLVED names
only. resolution.names is a property over the resolved set, so a miss never appears and
the span it covered is dropped from the prompt.
* no-registry branch (line 438): element_tags = list(names)  -- EVERY parsed name, so the
greedy name is re-emitted verbatim as a malformed tag.
So the precise rule is: the prose is eaten iff a registry is present AND the greedy name
misses, because element_tags is built from resolved names in that branch. The greedy parse
only mis-names; the REGISTRY BRANCH is what discards the span.
This graph ships no @/# tags of its own (the action text is a placeholder), so the trap does
not bite here -- but it will bite the first person who types a two-Element action line, and
it will take their direction with it.
REGISTRY PATH: this graph leaves CinemaPromptCompose.registry_path UNSET, which is safe
because all four registry-touching nodes share one default. Verified by AST, not assumed:
_default_registry_path() is called at nodes.py:1142 (CinemaElementSave), 1238
(CinemaElementLoad), 1281 (CinemaElementList) and 1995 (CinemaPromptCompose). Save, load,
list and compose therefore cannot silently split across two registry files.
THE IDENTITY-CONTINUITY PATH IS DELIBERATELY NOT USED. CinemaElementSave has no palette or
bbox input, so an Element it writes cannot feed elements.character_record_from_element(),
which raises rather than inventing a palette. Nodes 68 and 69 (ChorosContinuity,
CharacterContinuity) therefore take their shot list from a hand-written JSON primitive
(node 61), not from the registry. Nothing in this graph depends on that gap. Closing it
means adding palette/bbox to CinemaElementSave; until then the identity path is unreachable
from a graph, and this README says so rather than implying the registry feeds it.
READ FROM SOURCE -- the ten landed nodes, exactly as app/cinematographer/nodes.py declares
CinemaElementSave  <- name, category (ELEMENT_CATEGORIES), image_path | + description,
seed, registry_path  -> element_json, sidecar_path, summary
CinemaElementLoad  <- name, category | + registry_path
-> asset_path, element_json, found
CinemaElementList  <- category | + registry_path -> names_json, count, summary
CinemaGrade        <- the seven GRADE_PARAMS floats -> grade_json, is_neutral, summary
CinemaExtend       <- mode, duration_s, overlap_frames -> extend_json, overlap_s, summary
CinemaEdit         <- label, bbox_min_x, bbox_min_y, bbox_max_x, bbox_max_y, prompt
-> edit_json, in_frame, summary
Note what is NOT there on Extend and Edit: no IMAGE. CinemaGradeApply is the one node
that takes and returns an IMAGE, and CinemaGrade DOES take `corrections` -- an earlier
draft of this file said otherwise, from a read taken before the input landed.

Flux.1 [schnell] block   the official ComfyUI Flux.1 Schnell text-to-image graph, read

ATTRIBUTION DISCIPLINE, since this README quotes a source document. Every quotation and
every claim about the product below was grepped against
research/20-workflow-walkthrough.md (shipped in this repository), not
recalled -- a quotation is a claim, and a misattributed one is worse than a wrong slot
count because it is unfalsifiable at a glance.
THE CHECK IS TO GREP THE TIER, NOT THE WORDS. The walkthrough tags every sourced claim
with a provenance tier, and the tier is part of the claim: T1 is Higgsfield's own material
(docs.higgsfield.ai and the higgsfield.ai blog), while V1/V2/V3 are third-party reviewers
(Joseph Martin / Thomas Creates / Youri). The tier is printed on the line, usually in the
same sentence or the same table row. So: T1 means this README may say 'the product does';
V1/V2/V3 means it must name the reviewer. Grepping the words alone does not catch a tier
error, which is exactly why re-reading a quotation feels sufficient and is not.
Three tier errors were caught this way and are corrected in place rather than quietly:
- the 'empty of people' location technique is V3's (Youri's), a REVIEWER's, not the
product's -- see delta 5;
- the image model: the T1 catalogue lists SIX models and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst is the
tutorials' T3 preference, not a product mandate -- see BUILD and delta 1;
- the Stage 0 workspace claim carries the walkthrough's own '(b) claimed' grading,
because the one section recommending the product is the one section with zero visual
evidence (lines 86-88).
Where the source attributes something to a reviewer rather than to Higgsfield, this
README names the reviewer.
WHAT THE VALIDATOR CHECKS, AND WHAT IT STILL CANNOT. Worth stating plainly, because a PASS
is only as strong as the checks behind it and this one got stronger this turn. It checks:
JSON shape; that every class_type is in a table read from source; that every link resolves
to a real node and a declared output slot; that every node supplies the right NUMBER of
inputs; that every supplied input NAME is declared and every REQUIRED name is present; that
the graph is acyclic; and that every node is reachable from an output node.
The name check is new, and it earned its place immediately: it caught all four director
nodes wired with placeholder names the moment those nodes landed. A count check cannot catch
that, and did not.
It still CANNOT check, and this README will not pretend otherwise:
* input TYPES -- a STRING wired into an IMAGE input passes. Only ComfyUI's own
validate_node_input knows that, and this validator does not call it;
* widget VALUES -- 'Joy' vs 'joy' in an EMOTIONS combo, or a sampler name that does not
exist, passes here and fails at run time. The values in this graph were executed against
the engine, but nothing enforces that they stay legal;
* whether the graph RUNS. It has never been executed. Structural validation is not
execution, and no claim here should be read as one.
DELIBERATE DELTAS from the product, and only these:
1. Image mode is Flux.1 [schnell] rather than GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst. See BUILD above.
The tier matters and is stated there: the platform offers SIX image models (T1) and
GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst is the tutorials' pick (T3), not a product mandate. Flux 2 is
among the six, so this is a licence-driven choice inside the product's own model
surface rather than a substitution of something foreign. The product's image side is
the platform's general image surface, not a Cinema Studio enum set, so no
product-specific behaviour is lost here.
2. Stage 0 (Project) is not in the graph. A project is a workspace: folders, a brief,
shared access, a canvas. None of that is a graph concept, and the teardown's own note
is that the workspace claim has ZERO on-screen evidence in the reviews. It is the
app's job, not the graph's.
3. Stage 2 (MODE) is not a node. Switching from image mode to video mode is a UI state
change; this graph IS video mode. The BUILD stage above is the image half, inlined.
4. The `@Element` / `#move` tags are composed by CinemaPromptCompose, not typed by hand.
The product's syntax is the app's surface; the API's own reference tokens are
one-based <<<image_1>>> / <<<video_1>>> / <<<audio_1>>>. This graph emits the app
syntax, because that is what the entry is a rebuild of. A workflow built for the
product's API would need the tags rewritten -- a real portability limit, not hidden.
5. The character reference does NOT enter the video model. LTX 2.5 I2V takes one first
frame, and that frame is the location clean plate. The convention behind that is a
REVIEWER's, not the product's, and the distinction is kept here deliberately: it is
V3's (Youri's) technique, which the walkthrough records as "V3's convention for
locations" -- describe every location as "a real photo taken on a film set" and keep
it "completely empty of people because the characters get added in by the video model
later" [V3 01:38-01:41]. It is a good technique and we follow it. It is not a spec,
and an earlier draft of this README called it "the product's own convention", which
it is not. The character is carried into the shot by the @Tamsin tag in
the composed prompt and by the Element registry, not by a second image input. Wiring
the character sheet into the sampler as well would misrepresent what LTX 2.5 I2V
accepts.
6. The camera pose is solved, not typed. CinematographerAutoFrame solves a compliant
eye/target/focal-length triple geometrically in 24 iterations and reports whether it
converged. This is a superset of the product: Cinema Studio 4.0 DROPPED focal length
(a control in 1.0, absent from the 4.0 schema), and our engine has it as a
first-class parameter. The Director's Panel's body/lens/aperture selection is what
would inform that pose in a full build; here the pose is solved and the panel is
carried into the prompt, which is the honest split given that the panel's lens values
are hand-tuned character profiles with no published mapping to focal length.
7. Every diagnostic terminates in a PreviewAny node. This is not decoration: a ComfyUI
node whose output nothing consumes and which is not OUTPUT_NODE = True is PRUNED and
never executes, so a diagnostic that nothing reads is a diagnostic that never runs.
PreviewAny is a core output node, which is what makes the judge and the POST plans
actually execute. The app reads them from the node outputs.
8. Extend and Edit are local plan nodes, not Seedance 2.5 endpoint calls. In the real
product they are separate endpoints -- the API docs say so plainly -- so this is a
rebuild of the FEATURE's description, not of the call, and not of the pixels.
9. Sound is generated by LTX 2.5's own audio VAE and muxed by CreateVideo. The product
has a sound toggle; here the audio latent is always present, which is the simpler and
more honest wiring. Drop nodes 37 and 56 and the audio input on 57 for a silent cut.
10. filename_prefix -> cinematographer/*, to namespace our outputs.
11. The action prompt and the subject/scene JSON are obvious placeholders. If a generated
clip ever shows PLACEHOLDER_ACTION_DID_NOT_RUN, injection did not run; that is the
signal it is there for. The two image_path widgets are placeholders in the same way:
the app must set them to the paths SaveImage wrote, because CinemaElementSave stores
a path and never reads a file. That is the one place where the graph and the app have
to agree on a string, and it is a direct consequence of the engine being stdlib-only.
AN OPEN QUESTION, RECORDED NOT RESOLVED. `rosesfield`, a competing entry in this same
competition, ships `motion-guide-ltx-2-5`, which cross-loads the LTX 2.3 union-control
IC-LoRA onto LTX 2.5. Cross-loading 2.3 IC-LoRAs into 2.5 is documented as experimental
with degraded tracking. They ship it anyway. We have not tested it and neither has anyone
we can cite, so this graph does not do it and this README does not call it wrong. It is a
real, checkable difference between the two entries and it belongs in the record.
WHAT IS VERIFIED vs NOT:
VERIFIED      valid JSON; class_type + inputs on every node; every link resolves to an
existing node id and a declared output slot; every node supplies a legal
number of inputs; acyclic; every node reachable from an output node.
NOT VERIFIED  that ComfyUI accepts this prompt; that the four declared class_types exist
or have these signatures; that the weights are installed; that it produces
a clip; that the judgement agrees with a human. None of that has been run.
REQUIRED NODE PACKS (custom):
NONE. Every class_type in this graph is either ComfyUI core or part of this pack.
Notably it does NOT need ComfyUI-LTXVideo or ComfyUI-CrossViewWarp: LTX 2.5's IC-LoRAs
are not used, so the Lightricks pack is off the critical path, and there is no camera
move node from a third party -- the move stack is a Director's Panel value.

The five LTX 2.5 names are the verified ones from reshoot_ltx25.json, unchanged. LTX 2.5
weights are GATED on HuggingFace (Lightricks/LTX-2.5): click 'Agree and Access' once.
LICENCE. Flux.1 [schnell] is Apache-2.0. ComfyUI is GPL-3.0. LTX 2.5 weights are LTX-2.x
Community (revenue-capped) and gated. No Higgsfield logos, no likeness of any person, no
MiniMax H3, no closed API, no partner nodes, no network calls -- the graph is licence-clean
by construction and runs entirely locally. See reshoot_wan22_fun_control.json for the
Apache-2.0-only alternative to the LTX half.
MEASURED: nothing. No timing, no VRAM figure, no output, no cost. The product shows a
credit cost on its Generate button before you confirm; this graph has no cost to show,
because it does not call anything that charges.
